newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea offers Red Cross talks with North for aid.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea offers Red Cross talks with North for aid.

text.p: The South Korean Red Cross on Friday offered talks with the North Korean Red Cross to speed up food aid to the famine-threatened nation.

Kang Young-hoon, president of the South Korean Red Cross, proposed the talks for "speedy and smooth" delivery of food and other relief materials to his Northern counterpart, a Red Cross statement said.
The message was delivered via a "hot line" linking the two organisations.

It came two days after North Korean representatives demanded substantial international assistance at a meeting in New York with South Korean and U.S. diplomats called to hear Pyongyang's answer to a proposal for peace talks.
Seoul and Washington insist large-scale aid can only be discussed at four-nation peace talks, also including China.
The South Korean Red Cross has made 14 relief shipments since November 1995 to North Korea, including $1 million worth of potatoes and vegetable seed this month.
South Korean religious and other civic groups have pledged to raise $20 million to buy 110,000 tonnes of corn. All private aid shipments must be channeled through the Red Cross.
"I think it is desirable for South and North Korean Red Cross officials to meet and directly discuss speedy and smooth delivery of food and materials being sent to you," Kang said in the message.
He called for a meeting as soon as possible in Panmunjom, the only border-crossing point along the heavily-fortified Demilitarized Zone bisecting the Korean peninsula.
The national Red Cross has been shipping aid through the International Federation for Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies.

Separately, the United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) has appealed for $95.5 million for food aid. The United States has pledged $25 and South Korea $6 million, although Seoul is now mulling a larger donation.
Washington officials said on Thursday no new U.S. food aid pledges were expected before North Korea responded conclusively to the peace talks.

They said North Korea began Wednesday's crucial meeting in New York by essentially accepting a U.S.-South Korean proposal for talks but then tied acceptance to a new demand for international assistance.
Foreign ministry officials in Seoul said the North Korean demand prevented agreement at Wednesday's talks. A further session has been scheduled for Friday.
Both Seoul and Washington officials said they believed Pyongyang would eventually accept the peace talks.
The four-party talks are aimed at replacing a truce agreement that ended the 1950-53 Korean War with a lasting peace on the peninsula.
